body: The sun gets into 412 at a quarter past eight, through the one window, and lays itself across Theo’s half of the room first, because Theo’s half is where the good furniture is. Through the wall Doug’s alarm begins the argument it has with Doug every morning, a car horn on a nine-minute snooze, and loses.

Theo is at his desk, dressed, the blue blazer on and the Sigma Rho pin set into the lapel at the exact angle three brothers told him to. On the nightstand Hollis keeps his retirement in the teacup. “Hollis was concerned,” Theo says, to the MacBook, as Jack comes in. “I told him you’d been detained by the Holy See.”
Jack is in yesterday’s Mass shirt, untucked, under the Carhartt, which is not a look that has ever fooled anyone, least of all an egg.
“He’s an egg.”

“He is a *retired* egg, Costigan, and he keeps vigil. It’s all he has left.” Theo looks up then, with a question in his face, and Jack waits for it. Theo folds it small and puts it away somewhere inside the blazer. “Two words,” he says instead. “Seven hours after I asked. *Home. Eventually.* One of them is a hedge.”
“It was accurate.”

“It was a confession. Sit. Your Englishman wrote.” He turns the MacBook around on the desk. Jack has never owned a laptop, so his Marisol e-mail lives on Theo’s, in a second window, and behind it is a window with the President’s budget in it, $3.8 trillion and a three-year freeze, which Theo shuts as if it had asked him for money. “Saturday, to all twelve of you. I took the liberty. You didn’t check.”

He reads it aloud before Jack can, in Hale’s vowels, which he does well: the Oxford pressed flat like a flower between the clauses, and a pause after *ambitions* where Hale would take a sip of something.

body.title: PHIL 109H — Monday
body.text: For Monday, in place of what the syllabus says: Joyce, “The Dead.” It is a long story with ambitions. Read it twice. No sides; for once you will all simply read. —A.H.

body: “*No sides*,” Theo says, in his own voice, and sets the phrase down between them like a ceasefire. “Joyce. I have a copy, from a previous owner who found Gabriel Conroy SO CONDESCENDING, in green ink, and was correct. Don’t let her opinions near yours.” He gets the Penguin off the shelf over his bed and puts it in Jack’s hand. “Forty-odd pages, twice. It is the greatest short story in English and it has a goose in it, so pace yourself. You have five hours and, I’m told, a soul.”
The word *Wednesday* is in neither of them. They both go around it the way you cross a room with a full tray.
At the door, bag on his shoulder, blazer squared, Theo turns. “Six days, Costigan.”
Jack doesn’t ask till what. Everyone in Delgado can count to Sunday.

He reads at his desk with the door propped open, the way he read at Glenwood, with other people’s noise leaking in at the edges, and by the time Doug’s alarm has lost for the fourth time he has met a girl named Lily, who is already run off her feet, and a man named Gabriel, who is already worried about his speech.

s05.slug: MONDAY · 9:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE LETTER
body: 412 with Theo out is a different country: the speaker dark, one desk lamp, one yellow circle on the blotter, and through the wall the clatter of Doug in Northrend, in long patient bursts, killing something large.

The Gospel at the twelve-ten was the man in the tombs, and Jack has been carrying him around since noon. A man with a regiment inside him, sitting at Jesus’s feet clothed and in his right mind, begging to be taken along in the boat, and told no. *Go home to your family, and tell them.* Danny’s review of the passage, delivered at eleven from the third pew at St. Brigid’s in a whisper that reached the sanctuary, was the pigs: two thousand of them, over a cliff, and somebody owed a farmer.

Letters to Trumbull have a grammar, and Jack could recite it like the Baltimore Catechism: no staples, no stickers, no perfume, no crayon, no cardstock, no clippings, nothing that could have been soaked in anything. Every page also has a second reader, a corrections officer at a table in Leavittsburg with a rubber stamp and a cup of coffee, whom Danny refers to in his own letters only as the State of Ohio, as in *the State of Ohio would like you to know it enjoyed your description of kelp.* So Jack writes for two readers, and it turns out to be the best thing that ever happened to his prose. Nothing in it can be wet. Everything in it is a fact or a joke, and a joke will carry a fact past the State of Ohio without being searched.

He uncaps the pen. Delgado stationery, cream, with the seal on it; block capitals, because that is how Danny writes to him, and a letter ought to answer in the language it was sent in. There is one sentence near the bottom that he writes twice. He draws three hard strokes through the first, and writes it again directly underneath, the same words in the same capitals, and leaves it there.

body.title: A letter, Delgado Hall stationery
body.text:
DAN —
HAPPY BIRTHDAY. 23. CANDLEMAS, WHICH NONNA SAYS MAKES YOU HOLY BY ACCIDENT.
THERE’S A BOX COMING FROM A STORE ON STATE STREET, BECAUSE THE CO’S LIKE IT BETTER FROM A STORE. A GIRL PICKED IT. SHE HAS OPINIONS ABOUT THE GRANDMOTHER. YOU’LL SEE.
THE BROWNS KEPT MANGINI. POP WILL HAVE THOUGHTS. LET HIM.
NONNA’S AT TWO CANDLES FOR MARIA CATERINA. SHE’S NEVER MET HER. THAT’S NONNA.
YOU ASKED ME SOMETHING AT CHRISTMAS. I THINK I’VE GOT IT.
— PROFESSOR (J.)

body: He had *Skye* in the third line and took it out. Danny has her name already, by way of Gina, who forwards names like a switchboard, and the State of Ohio can do without.

The envelope is a glossy one from the bookstore’s ten-pack, and the pen skips on it. DANIEL COSTIGAN, and the number, A555218, which he knows the way he knows his birthday; TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION; LEAVITTSBURG, OHIO 44430. Every letter goes down in a small bead of ink that he drags along with the side of his hand, and when he rubs his face with that hand, because it is ten to ten and he has been up since a window on Del Playa went gold, the ink goes where the hand goes.
It wants a stamp, and sealing, and a place to be finished. The Fishbowl is lit downstairs and the hall up here is going quiet, and he can have either.

choices.text: Take it down to the Fishbowl.
response: He wants people around him and doesn’t say so. The Fishbowl is lit.
He stays at the desk with the window open and the hall going quiet.

s05f.slug: MONDAY · 10:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: At ten the Fishbowl’s glass wall has stopped being a window and become a mirror, so that Jack, coming down the corridor with an envelope, meets a boy in a Carhartt coming toward him with an envelope, and the two of them reach the door together and have to let each other in.

Margot has the long table, with a mug of tea sweating on her notebook and, between her knuckles, a clove cigarette she is not permitted to light indoors, which she turns end over end like a drum major. Doug has the near end, a laptop and a Hot Pocket whose second half is cooling in its sleeve. Kevin sits across from him with the orgo text open, a highlighter behind his ear, his BlackBerry face down on his notes. Over the vending alcove the television plays a panel of men in ties in total silence, under a crawl that says $3.8 TRILLION, and then THREE-YEAR FREEZE, and then a basketball score. The room is not watching it.

“Six,” Margot says, as Jack sits, as though they were in the middle of the sentence. “Six versions of Wednesday are now in circulation in this building. The sixth arrived this afternoon from the Classics department, which has given it a chorus.”
“A chorus.”
“Strophe, antistrophe. I’m told the dog has the best lines.”
“Read me one.”

“I don’t distribute primary sources.” She tips the clove at him. “You’d start correcting them, Costigan, and then they’d be yours. I will tell you that every version has two principals and a dog, and that where they differ is in whom the dog likes.”
“The dog likes everyone. The dog is deaf.”
“That,” Margot says, “is the first accurate sentence anyone has contributed in a week, and I resent that it came from a participant.”
Doug raises a hand from his Hot Pocket. “The one where the dog bit Costigan is mine.”
“It has acquired a limp,” Margot says.
“It’s *evolved*. He got bit at the *table*.”
“The dog was nowhere near the table.”
“Dude,” Doug says, with the patience of the wronged, “that’s what the dog would *say*.”

Jack lays the envelope on the table. It faces Kevin, upside down, in capitals: TRUMBULL, and the number. Kevin’s eyes go over it once at the speed of someone reading a menu he knows, and come away, and the highlighter goes on moving. Jack pats his pockets for the stamps Ma packed in August and remembers where they are, which is on his desk, upstairs, doing nothing. Kevin’s hand goes to his back pocket. He produces a single stamp in a glassine sleeve out of a wallet that has a place for everything, and slides it across the laminate, without looking up.
“Thanks, Kev.”

“Don’t thank me,” Kevin tells the page. “It’s the first thing anybody’s needed from me tonight that I could actually supply.” He underlines something. “Clare’s grandfather’s violin is Czech, by the way. A hundred years old, and in better tune than the nine-thirty band, which I say with love, because I’m in it.”
Jack presses the stamp on, which takes two tries on glossy paper, and licks the flap. It tastes like the bookstore’s glue and a little like the pen.
“Mailing something to Ohio by hand,” Margot says, to the clove. “You’re a nineteenth-century man, Costigan.”
“Eighteen.”
“Till March. I have the date.”
He takes the stairs up with the envelope in his coat, and on the fourth-floor landing the lounge light is on, laying a yellow rectangle across the carpet as far as the stairwell door.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them.

body: By ten the hall has gone the way Delgado goes on a Monday, doors shutting in order from the elevator end, until all that’s left of the floor is Doug’s keyboard through the wall and the window Jack has propped four inches, which lets in the cold and the eucalyptus, in that order. At half past, Priya makes her rounds, one knock per door and the same sentence in the same key, *quiet hours are not suggestions*, and to 412, whose door is open, she says it twice and adds, to the room at large, “I’m going to need that door to commit.”

On the pillow the Penguin lies face down at the goose. The RAZR sits beside the lamp, quiet; she has lines to run for a tape she won’t name yet, and he believes her. He reads the letter over once and changes nothing. Then he goes through the duffel under the bed for a stamp and finds the book Ma packed in August, in the front pocket, with a Post-it on it in her St. Brigid’s secretary’s hand that says LETTERS. She packed a book of twenty. There are four left. Ma, who can audit a household by its stamps, will want to know who got the other sixteen, and the answer, mostly, is Danny.

At twenty to eleven Theo comes in, in shirtsleeves, the blazer over his arm and the pin clipped to the lapel, and stops at the sight of the envelope on the blotter. He reads the address from where he stands. “Is it tomorrow?”
“Tomorrow.”
“Twenty-three.” He considers it. “Tell the man the hat is holding up. It survived pledge week with its dignity, which is more than I can say for the Browns’ secondary.”
“I’ll tell him.”

Theo crosses to his desk, opens the drawer, and takes out a yellow legal pad written over from margin to margin, and holds it against his chest, face in. “Study group,” he says. “Laney’s. Statistics. There’s a thermos, and a professor’s old midterm.”
“You’ve never been in a study group.”
“I’m diversifying.” He is gone before the drawer has finished sliding shut.

With Theo out the room goes back to itself. Rosie’s Christmas drawing has slipped on its tack again, Jack very tall beside a crab the size of a dog and a tree with a star bigger than either of them, and he puts it straight with his thumb. Over his narrow bed the crucifix. Over Theo’s desk the princes Rosie drew him, which Theo taped up at Christmas and has defended ever since against all comers; in the frame of Theo’s mirror, Nonna’s twenty. On the sill the porch on Glenwood in a drugstore print, with Ma’s thumb in one corner. On the nightstand, in his teacup, Hollis, at rest.
He stamps the envelope with Ma’s stamp, and it goes on crooked, and he lets it. Her book of twenty is down to three. Through the wall Doug kills the large thing a second time, with feeling.
At a quarter past eleven he turns off the lamp, picks the envelope up off the blotter, and goes out.

s05a.slug: MONDAY · 11:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — TWO LEGAL PADS

body.text: Coming back up from the Fishbowl with the stamped envelope, Jack passes the lounge at the end of the fourth floor, and the door is open.
body.else: On his way down the hall to the stairs with the stamped envelope, Jack passes the lounge, and the door is open.

body: The television is dark and the vending machine is humming to itself. Two yellow legal pads lie side by side on the coffee table, each written over in a different hand, one spiky and slanting, one round, with circles over its *i*’s. On the carpet in front of them kneel Theo, in shirtsleeves, and Laney, in a Pi Lam sweatshirt and plaid pajama pants, with a pencil holding up her hair, each with one finger moving down one page, in time, line by line, like two people proofreading.
“…they can’t *both* be…” Laney is saying.
“…same night, Laney. Same *phone* —”
“Don’t you *Laney* me in that voice, Theodore. I’m working.”
Laney’s pad is face down before Jack has finished stopping. Theo’s follows half a second behind, with more grace and less speed.
“Wedding seating chart,” Theo says. “Hypothetical. Round tables, eight to a table. Nobody is speaking to the bride’s aunt.”
“The aunt,” Laney says, “has been through a great deal. And the groom’s people are Methodists, so they go by the exits, and near a pie.”
“Whose wedding?” Jack says.
“Hypothetical people,” says Laney. “They’re very happy.”

“They are *not* happy,” says Theo. “Their families have met. We’ve put the bride’s father by the open bar, which is the Christian thing, and the best man at the children’s table for reasons of national security.”

body.text:
“I thought it was a study group,” Jack says.

“The wedding is for the study group,” Theo says, without a flicker. “It’s a very large study.”

body: “You have ink on your face, Costigan,” Theo adds, changing the subject at once and with visible relief.

Laney gets up off the carpet. She has been cold to Jack for a month in a way that has rules, civil, exact, a *good morning* delivered at the right interval and a *Jack* with nothing on it, and now she crosses the room in her socks and looks at the side of his face. “Hold still.”
“I’m holding.”

“You are doing the opposite of holding.” She licks her thumb, there is no other way to say it, and takes something off his cheekbone in three brisk strokes, like a pageant mother going after lipstick on a front tooth. It is the first time Laney has touched him since January, and it is with saliva. She turns the thumb to the lamp. It is black at the tip. “Ink,” she says, and wipes it on Theo’s sleeve, and Theo says “*Hey*,” and she is already walking back to the carpet. “Night, sugar.”

Jack takes it, if he takes it at all, for the two of them going over Hale’s again, for Lena’s sake. He had his share of Lena at one o’clock, and the share is spent. He stays in the doorway long enough to see that the pads are going to stay face down for as long as he does, and goes. In 412 the envelope goes against the lamp, to ride down with him in the morning.

Theo comes in at twenty to twelve without the legal pad, and gets into bed in his shirt and trousers, and the room is dark but for the stairwell light under the door. Jack lies on top of the blanket and finds Hollis on the nightstand by the shape of the teacup.
“What are you doing the week of the seventh?” Theo says, to the ceiling.
“Working.”
“Hm.”
“Why?”
“No reason. Seven is a number your people like. Sacraments, sorrows, deadly sins. I’m a student of the form.”
Through the wall Doug’s tauren dies, loudly, and Doug says so.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again.
